## 18 Coupling to external models via Basic Model Interface (BMI)

This chapter is on the *coupling* of hydrodynamics to external models. When running a coupled model the DIMR program takes care of the exchange of data between components, and each component will be addressed using BMI calls. Section 18.1 contains the technical details of the D-Flow FM implementation of the BMI.

The other sections of this chapter go into more detail for a specific external model: coupling with D-Waves in section 18.6, coupling to D-RTC in section 18.7, and coupling to D-SLE (Sea Lock Exchange) in section 18.8.

### 18.1 BMI interface to interact with the D-Flow FM model state

The D-Flow FM kernel shared library offers an API that implements the Basic Model Interface (BMI). The BMI allows one to initialize, run, and finalize a model component via standardized interface calls; furthermore it allows one to get and set various quantities such that model components can dynamically react to the computed results. General details on the BMI can be found in Peckham *et al.* (2013). This section discusses some of the D-Flow FM specifics.

Many variables in D-Flow FM's model state can be inquired and changed via BMI calls. Setting a variable can be done via a call to `set_var(varname, userdata)`, which copies the data from the `userdata` array to the D-Flow FM memory associated with the `varname` variable. Alternatively, one may use a call to `get_var(varname, xptr)`, which returns a pointer to the requested variable, and directly assign new values to the D-Flow FM memory from outside the running simulation. The latter approach may be faster because less data needs to be copied.

### 18.2 DIMR and the BMI

The DIMR program takes care of the exchange of data between components, and each component will be addressed using BMI calls. The data to be exchanged is defined in the `<dimr.xml>` configuration file, under the `<dimrConfig><coupler><item>` elements. More details on DIMR can be found in Deltares (2026).

The variable names specified there need to be supported by the addressed component. For instance, for the coupling to D-RTC (see Section 18.7) typically scalar quantities need to be exchanged that are defined at specific locations (such as observation points or structures). Since BMI only identifies variables by a unique variable name without any location selection, D-Flow FM identifies both location and quantity by introducing *compound* variable names (not to be confused with a compound structure). A compound variable name takes the form:

```
varname = "groupname/locationid/fieldname"
```

For example the variable name "weirs/Lith01/CrestLevel" will select the crest level at the weir named "Lith01".

The `groupname` part of the variable name identifies the location or object type. Currently known group names are listed below. Unless noted otherwise, please check Section 18.3 for the list of quantities supported for those groups of locations.

- ◊ pumps
- ◊ weirs
- ◊ gates

- ◇ general structures
- ◇ source sinks
- ◇ observations (observation points, see Section 18.4)
- ◇ cross sections (observation cross sections, see Section 18.4)
- ◇ laterals (see Section 18.5)

The locationid part of the variable name is the unique identifier of the intended object. More details on the specific identifier used can be found in the subsequent sections on the various object groups. The fieldname identifies the quantity at the selected location. Which quantities are supported depends on the groupname.

### 18.3 BMI access to hydraulic structure data in D-Flow FM

To access quantities defined at structures use a compound variable name as explained in Section 18.2. The locationid part of the compound variable name is, for hydraulic structures, equal to the id key in the structure input file (Table C.23). Which quantities can be addressed via the BMI, depends on the structure type indicated by the groupname. Table 18.1 lists the supported field names for each hydraulic structure group.

**Table 18.1:** Supported compound variable fields for hydraulic structures in D-Flow FM via BMI.

| Group name         | Field name           | Access     | Remark                                                                            |
|--------------------|----------------------|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| pumps              | Capacity             | read-write | Only for non-staged pumps. Prescribed capacity, not necessarily actual discharge. |
|                    | weirs                | CrestLevel | read-write                                                                        |
| gates              | CrestLevel           | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | GateHeight           | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | GateLowerEdgeLevel   | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | GateOpeningWidth     | read-write |                                                                                   |
| general structures | CrestLevel           | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | GateHeight           | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | GateLowerEdgeLevel   | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | GateOpeningWidth     | read-write |                                                                                   |
| longculverts       | ValveRelativeOpening | read-write |                                                                                   |
|                    | source sinks         | Discharge  | read-write                                                                        |
|                    | ChangeInSalinity     | read-write | Prescribed change, not necessarily actual change.                                 |
|                    | ChangeInTemperature  | read-write | Prescribed change, not necessarily actual change.                                 |

**18.4 BMI access to observations in D-Flow FM**To access quantities defined at observation points and observation cross sections use a compound variable name as explained in Section 18.2. The `locationid` for observation points should match the `name` specified in the relevant input file (See Section E.2.2). All observation point names must be unique when accessing the data via BMI. The same holds for the `locationid` for observation cross sections (See Section E.2.4).

Table 18.2 lists the supported field names for each observation group. All supported variables/fields are read-only, evidently, as observations are only 'observing' the flow. Typically, these variables are used as input to hydraulic triggers in an RTC-coupling.

**Table 18.2: Supported compound variable fields for observations in D-Flow FM via BMI.**

| Group name    | Field name                      | Access    | Remark                                       |
|---------------|---------------------------------|-----------|----------------------------------------------|
| observations  |                                 |           |                                              |
|               | <code>water_level</code>        | read-only | Observation points                           |
|               | <code>water_depth</code>        | read-only |                                              |
|               | <code>velocity</code>           | read-only |                                              |
|               | <code>discharge</code>          | read-only |                                              |
|               | <code>salinity</code>           | read-only | Only when salinity transport is on.          |
|               | <code>temperature</code>        | read-only | Only when temperature transport is on.       |
|               | <code>&lt;tracername&gt;</code> | read-only | Only when that named tracer is in the model. |
| crosssections |                                 |           |                                              |
|               | <code>discharge</code>          | read-only | Space-integrated along cross section.        |
|               | <code>velocity</code>           | read-only | Space-averaged along cross section.          |
|               | <code>water_level</code>        | read-only | Space-averaged along cross section.          |
|               | <code>water_depth</code>        | read-only | Space-averaged along cross section.          |

**Remarks:**

- ◇ In 3D models, BMI access to 3D quantities is currently still very rudimentary. D-Flow FM's BMI API provides a pointer to the *first* layer. This means that for sigma models, the value at the bottom layer is returned. For z-layers this will only be the actual bottom layer value if that particular location has its bed level in layer number 1. For shallower locations where layer number 1 is inactive, only a dummy fill value is returned.
- ◇ When using `get_var()` a pointer is returned, which allows reading values in higher layers (using offset "layer index  $\times$  8 bytes"). This requires expert knowledge; it is not available in DIMR-based couplings.
- ◇ This holds for salinity, temperature, `<tracername>` and also velocity and discharge.

**18.5 BMI access to forcings in D-Flow FM**To access quantities defined as local forcings (currently only lateral discharges) use a compound variable name as explained in Section 18.2. The `locationid` for lateral discharges should match the `id` specified for them in the external forcings input (See Section C.6.3.2). Table 18.3 lists the supported field names for each forcing group.

**Table 18.3:** Supported compound variable fields for forcings in D-Flow FM via BMI.

| Group name | Field name                | Access     | Remark                                                                                                     |
|------------|---------------------------|------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| laterals   |                           |            |                                                                                                            |
|            | water_discharge           | read-write | Prescribed discharge, not necessarily actual discharge (when negative).                                    |
|            | water_level               | read-only  | Water level, averaged value over the nodes in the lateral.                                                 |
|            | water_volume              | read-only  | Total water volume per layer, for each lateral.                                                            |
|            | water_discharge_per_layer |            |                                                                                                            |
|            |                           | read-write | Prescribed discharge, distributed over the layers.                                                         |
|            | incoming/<constituent>    | read-write | Concentration of a transported quantity in incoming direction, array with 1 value per layer.               |
|            | outgoing/<constituent>    | read-only  | Concentration of a transported quantity in outgoing direction, averaged value over the lateral, per layer. |

**Remark:**

- ◇ <constituent> can be water\_salinity, water\_temperature or <tracername>.

**18.6 Coupling with D-Waves (SWAN)**This section is on the *coupling* of hydrodynamics and waves. Full documentation on D-Waves is available in its own User Manual; this section is limited to the details of running coupled flow-wave models, and the physical interaction processes between the two of them.

**Restriction:**

- ◇ D-Flow FM runs integrated with D-Waves provided that only triangles or quadrangles are applied in the D-Flow FM model grid. In case of pentagons or hexagons a coupling with D-Waves isn't possible.

We remark that a coupled flow-wave model always consists of the combination of a hydrodynamic model with an unstructured grid (D-Flow FM) coupled to a wave model with a structured grid (SWAN). D-Flow FM cannot be coupled yet to a wave model with a unstructured grid (for example UNSWAN).

**18.6.1 Getting started**With respect to waves, *offline* and *online* results into:

1. 1 *offline*: First, a separate D-Waves computation is executed, resulting in a communication file (com-file) containing wave data. Then a D-Flow FM computation is executed, using the wave data from the com-file.
2. 2 *online*: D-Flow FM computations are alternated with D-Waves calculations. D-Flow FM writes flow data to the com-file, D-Waves uses this flow data for the wave calculation and writes wave data to the com-file. D-Flow FM uses the updated wave data.

file prescribes the mode and when the D-Flow FM computation should be paused to perform a D-Waves calculation. From within the working directory, the following run-scripts in the installation directory can be called:

◇ On Windows:

<Your installation base dir>\x64\bin\run\_dimr.bat

◇ On Linux:

<Your installation base dir>/lnx64/bin/run\_dimr.sh

◇ On Windows, a computation with D-Flow FM in parallel using MPI:

<Your installation base dir>\x64\bin\run\_dimr\_parallel.bat

◇ On Linux, submitting a job on the Deltares cluster (sequential and parallel):

<Your installation base dir>/lnx64/bin/submit\_dimr.sh

This script can be used for clusters outside Deltares too, but system specific modifications will be needed.

**Note:** Example models, with run scripts, are included in the (open source) code. After registering yourself at <https://oss.deltares.nl/>, you can have a look at: [https://svn.oss.deltares.nl/repos/delft3d/trunk/examples/12\\_dflowfm/test\\_data/e100\\_f02\\_c02-FriesianInlet\\_schematic\\_FM\\_wave](https://svn.oss.deltares.nl/repos/delft3d/trunk/examples/12_dflowfm/test_data/e100_f02_c02-FriesianInlet_schematic_FM_wave)

### 18.6.2 Input D-Flow FM

Optionally add the following lines to the .mdu file:

```
[numerics]
Epshu           = 0.05  # Input for threshold water depth for wet and dry cells
[waves]
Wavemodelnr    = 3       # Wave model nr, 0=no, 1=fetch/depth limited hurdlestive,
                        2=youngverhagen, 3 = D-Waves, 4=wave group forcing
Rouwav           = FR84
Gammax           = 1.0       # Maximum wave height/water depth ratio
waveSwartDelwaq = 0       # Communicate bed shear stress to D-Water Quality.
                        0=Parametrization WCI Soulsby (1997) using Rouwav;
                        1=linear sum taucur+tauwav;
                        2=morphological bed shear stress. Default 0.[output]
ComInterval = 1200.                              # (Fixed) Interval with which the wave
                                                        communication file is written for
                                                        wavemodelnr=3. Default: dtuser
ComOutputTimeVector = compoints.ctv                   # File with number of
                                                        prefixed communication
                                                        timepoints, only for wavemodelnr=3EulerVelocities = 1                                   # 0 (default): GLM, 1: Euler.
Only relevant when using waves
```

Description:

| Wavemodelnr     | Key switch to enable wave modelling. Use “3” for wave data from D-Waves (online or offline) and passing hydrodynamic data to D-Waves (online only). A file will be generated automatically named <“runid”_com.nc> to exchange data. |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Rouwav          | Necessary to include bed shear-stress enhancement by waves. See also Delft3D-FLOW manual.                                                                                                                                           |
| EulerVelocities | Optional flag to write Eulerian velocities to the D-Flow FM map file. Currently, only Eulerian values will be written for the cell centre veloc-                                                                                    |

- Epshu ity x-component and y-component (parameters ucx and ucy). Check that the "long\_name" contains the word "Eulerian".  
  Optionally overwrite the default value of "1.0e-4". Depending on your model, the default value of Epshu in combination with modelling waves may lead to huge local velocities near (almost) dry points. This will result in very small time steps. Increasing Epshu might be a reasonable workaround.
- Gammax Optionally overwrite the default value of "1.0". Depending on your model, the default value of Gammax may lead to huge local velocities in shallow water. Decreasing Gammax might be a reasonable workaround.
- waveSwartDelwaq Optional flag to communicate bed shear stresses from Delft3D-FLOW to D-Water Quality. Possible values are 0, 1 or 2. Only applicable if `wavemodelnr>0`. The default is set to 0. If `waveSwartDelwaq` equals 0, the bed shear stress is taken from the flow model. In practice, this means that the wave-current interaction is parametrized according to (Soulsby, 1997) and the resulting bed shear stress is communicated to D-Water Quality. A simpler approach is obtained using `waveSwartDelwaq` equal to 1. In that case, the shear stress that is communicated is the linear sum of the bed shear stress due to currents and the shear stress due to waves. In case of `waveSwartDelwaq` equal to 2, the maximum shear stress over the wave cycle (Soulsby, 1997) is communicated.
- ComInterval Optional entry to set the interval with which the communication file to D-Waves is written. When this is not specified, the communication file is written with DtUser intervals. Can be specified as an array: interval, start time, stop time in seconds since RefDate. Not compatible with ComOutputTimeVector.
- ComOutputTimeVector Optional entry to the file (.ctv) containing fixed time points to write the communication file for the online wave coupling. Can be used in combination with varying DIMR communication time points (Section 18.6.4). Time points in seconds since RefDate. Not compatible with ComInterval.

### 18.6.3 Input D-Waves

Optionally add the following lines to the .mdw file:

| [Output]              |                                  |
|-----------------------|----------------------------------|
| MapWriteNetCDF        | = true                           |
| COMFile               | = ../fm/dflowfmoutput/fff_com.nc |
| NetCDFSinglePrecision | = false                          |
| locationFile          | = ../fm/loo_obs.xyn              |
| writeTable            | = true                           |

#### Description:

- MapWriteNetCDF Default value "false", resulting in no output written in netCDF format. The coupling with D-Flow FM is only implemented for netCDF format, so this flag must be set to "true" when being coupled with D-Flow FM.
- COMFile Necessary reference to the file being used to communicate data to and from D-Flow FM. The name must exactly match with the name of the com-file being generated by D-Flow FM.

|              | NetCDFSinglePrecision                                                                                                                                                                     | Optional flag to write data in single precision instead of double precision. Default value is “false”. Might be useful to decrease the size of the com-file or to compare with a Delft3D-FLOW computation. |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| locationFile | Optional reference to observation points in D-Flow FM. When in combination with the “writeTable” flag, D-Waves will produce a history file in netCDF format for these observation points. |                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| writeTable   | Optional flag to force SWAN to produce an output file in table format for each set of locations specified in a locationFile. Default value is “false”.                                    |                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

### 18.6.4 Input DIMR

Both D-Flow FM and D-Waves are used as dynamic libraries (DLL's on Windows, so's on Linux). DIMR is a small executable steering both dynamic libraries. Its input file, usually called “dimr\_config.xml”, looks like this:

```
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="iso-8859-1"?>
<dimrConfig xmlns="http://schemas.deltares.nl/dimrConfig"
                    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
                    xsi:schemaLocation="http://schemas.deltares.nl/dimrConfig"
                    http://content.oss.deltares.nl/schemas/d_hydro-1.00.xsd">
<documentation>
                    <fileVersion>1.00</fileVersion>
                    <createdBy>Deltares, Coupling team</createdBy>
                    <creationDate>2015-05-20T07:56:32+01</creationDate>
                    </documentation>                    <control>
                    <parallel>
                                <startGroup>
                                                    <time>0.0 60.0 99999999.0</time>
                                                    <coupler name="flow2rtc"/>
                                                    <start name="myNameRTC"/>
                                                    <coupler name="rtc2flow"/>
                                                    </startGroup>
                                                    <startGroup>
                                                    <time>0.0 3600.0 99999999.0</time>
                                                    <start name="myNameWave"/>
                                                    </startGroup>
                                                    <start name="myNameDFlowFM"/>
                                                    </parallel>
                    </control>                    <component name="myNameDFlowFM">
                                                    <library>dflowfm</library>
                                                    <process>0 1 2</process>
                                                    <mpiCommunicator>DFM_COMM_DFMWORLD</mpiCommunicator>
                                                    <workingDir>fm</workingDir>
                                                    <inputFile>weirtimeseries.mdu</inputFile>
                                                    <setting key="verbose" value="INFO"/>
                    </component>
                    <component name="myNameWave">
                                                    <library>wave</library>
                                                    <process>0</process>
                                                    <workingDir>wave</workingDir>
                                                    <!-- component specific -->
                                                    <inputFile>weir.mdw</inputFile>
                    </component>
                    <component name="myNameRTC">
                                                    <library>RTCTools_BMI</library>
                                                    <process>0</process>
                                                    <workingDir>rtc</workingDir>
                                                    <!-- component specific -->
                                                    <inputFile>.</inputFile>
```

```
</component><coupler name="flow2rtc">
    <sourceComponent>myNameDFlowFM</sourceComponent>
    <targetComponent>myNameRTC</targetComponent>
    <item>
        <sourceName>observations/Upstream/water_level</sourceName>
        <targetName>input_ObservationPoint01_water_level</targetName>
        </item>
    </coupler>
    <coupler name="rtc2flow">
        <sourceComponent>myNameRTC</sourceComponent>
        <targetComponent>myNameDFlowFM</targetComponent>
        <item>
            <sourceName>output_weir_crest_level</sourceName>
            <targetName>weirs/weir01/crest_level</targetName>
        </item>
    </coupler>
</dimrConfig>
```

#### Description:

- <control> Specifies the workflow of the deltaresHydro executable. It indicates which components are started in which order. If the data transfer is to be arranged by the main program DIMR, then a coupler should be included. The main <control> block is a sequential block; this means that each component is initialized, time stepped, and finalized before the next component starts. For each component/coupler listed inside the <control> block there will be a corresponding component/coupler specification block defined below.
- <parallel> Within a <parallel> tag the components are started concurrently (if the mpi process id's listed per component don't overlap) or executed synchronously in sequence (first all initialize, then time stepping, and to conclude all finalization calls). The order of the components is retained.
- <start> A <parallel> block contains exactly one <start> component, defining the start and end time of the simulation. This is the component inside the <parallel> block with the smallest time step and can be denoted as the "master-component". All other components must be defined with a <startGroup> and can be denoted as a "slave-component".
- <startGroup> A <startGroup> should be used if a component (possibly including couplers) should only be executed at a subset of simulation time steps.
- <time> Start-, step- and stop-time (in seconds) at which this slave-component should be executed. The times are relative to the times of the master-component. Thus a start-time of 0.0 always refers to the start time of the master-component and a stop-time of "infinity" always refers to the end time of the master-component.

*Alternative:* Instead of specifying start-, step- and stop-time it is also an option to specify the name of a tim-file containing all times for which this slave-component should be executed. Example line in file "dimr\_config.xml":

```
<time>wave_computations.tim</time>
```

Example content of file "wave\_computations.tim":

```
10800.0
14400.0
16200.0
```

#### Restrictions:

- ◇ The times in the tim-file must be in increasing order
- ◇ The times in the tim-file are relative to the times of the master-component
- ◇ The tim-file must contain at least 3 times

---

**<component name="myComponentName">** Component specification block. "myComponentName" is free to be defined by the user. It must match exactly with the reference in the <control> block above. The name of a component must be unique.

**<library>** Reference to the component to be executed. Currently "flowfm", "wave" and "FBCTools\_BMI" are supported. The name must match exactly the name of the related dll/so (excluding prefixes (e.g. "lib") and suffixes (e.g. ".dll" or ".so")). The library should be located in the search path, or it may include an absolute or relative path. Multiple <component> blocks may refer to the same component to be executed.

**<process>** Optional list of the ids of the mpi processes that should be used to run the component. If not specified, then the component will run only in process "0" (i.e. non-parallel). The processes may be specified as a space separated list with series compressed using colons e.g. "16:31" represents processes "16 17 18" up to "31".

**<mpiCommunicator>** D-Flow FM specific flag. Mandatory only when this D-Flow FM component should run a parallel (partitioned) model. Note that this is *unrelated* to the <parallel> tag as introduced above.

**<workingDir>** Specification of the working directory of this <component>, relative to the location of the "dimr\_config.xml" file. The workingDir is the base/root directory of all input and output files for the component. All other files will be located RELATIVE TO this folder. If not specified, then workingDir will be equal to the folder of the configuration file.

**<inputFile>** Specification of the input file of this <component>, relative to <workingDir>: D-Flow FM: mdu-file, D-Waves: mdw-file, D-RTC: .

**<coupler name="myCouplerName">** Coupler specification block. "myCouplerName" is free to be defined by the user. It must match exactly with the reference in the <control> block above. The name of a coupler must be unique.

**<sourceComponent>** Identifies which component provides the data.

**<targetComponent>** Identifies which component needs to receive the data. The coupler runs on the superset of the processes configured for the source and target components.

**<item>** For each quantity to be exchanged, the name in the source component and the name in the target component are specified. To support recursive components, a directory syntax is used with forward slashes. If a name includes a forward slash, then it needs to be escaped using a backward slash, like \;; if a name includes a backward slash, then it needs to be escaped with a backward slash, like \\.

**<sourceName>** Identifies which parameter will be sent at the source component side.

**<targetName>** Identifies which parameter will be received at the target component side.

**<setting>** DIMR way to provide the command line options in the form of key - value pairs. Currently only support for the keys processlibrary, bloomspecies and verbose.

**18.6.5 Online process order**When D-Flow FM runs online in alternation with D-Waves and D-RTC, process steps can be identified, where the order as prescribed in "dimr\_config.xml" is respected as much as possible. The process order of the example "dimr\_config.xml" file in the section above is:

1. 1 D-Flow FM : : Init  
   D-Flow FM is initialized. Grid- and Flow-data is written to the netCDF com-file.  
   Even though D-Flow FM is not the first component in the example config-file, it must be the first component to be initialized, because the initialization results may be needed when other components are initialized. This is implemented as an exceptional rule: The master-component is always the first component to be initialized.
2. 2 D-RTC : : Init  
   D-RTC is initialized using (only) D-RTC input. Data from other components is not initialized yet; default values are used.
3. 3 D-Waves : : Init  
   D-Waves is initialized. Grid- and Flow-data created by D-Flow FM : : Init is read from the com-file. Grid conversion factors are generated. The factors for the conversion from the (structured!) wave grid to the (unstructured) flow grid are calculated inside D-Waves. The factors for the conversion from the (unstructured) flow grid to the (structured) wave grid are calculated by "ESMF\_RegridWeightGen" via the execution of script <ESMF\_-RegridWeightGen\_in\_Delft3D-WAVE.bat> (Windows) or <ESMF\_RegridWeightGen\_in\_-Delft3D-WAVE.sh> (Linux).
4. 4 D-RTC : : Step  
   A D-RTC computation is performed at time "0.0": Data is communicated (by DIMR) from D-Flow FM to D-RTC, the actual D-RTC computation is executed, data is communicated (by DIMR) from D-RTC to D-Flow FM.
5. 5 D-Waves : : Step  
   A D-Waves calculation is performed at time "0.0": Flow data is read (by D-Waves) from the com-file and converted to the wave grid(s). SWAN input files are written, a SWAN calculation is started by executing script <swan.bat> (Windows) or <swan.sh> (Linux), SWAN output files are read, wave-data is converted to the flow grid and written to the com-file (by D-Waves).
6. 6 D-Flow FM : : Step  
   A D-Flow FM calculation is performed: The com-file is checked for wave data to be used/updated. The simulation time will proceed from "0.0" to "60.0" (next time that another component should be executed). Flow-data is written to the com-file (by D-Flow FM).
7. 7 D-RTC : : Step, D-Flow FM : : Step  
   A D-RTC computation is performed after every "60.0" seconds. Then a D-Flow FM computation is performed and the simulation time will proceed another "60.0" seconds. This continues until the simulation time has progressed for "3600.0" seconds.
8. 8 D-RTC : : Step, D-Waves : : Step, D-Flow FM : : Step  
   A D-RTC computation is performed, then a D-Waves computation, then a D-Flow FM computation. The simulation time will proceed another "60.0" seconds and the next D-RTC computation can start.
9. 9 D-RTC : : Finish  
   D-RTC is finished at the end of the simulation.
10. 10 D-Waves : : Finish  
    D-Waves is finished at the end of the simulation.
11. 11 D-Flow FM : : Finish  
    D-Flow FM is finished at the end of the simulation.

### 18.6.6 Related files

Below is an overview of the related files in the default directory structure. In this example the runid is set to `foo`.

```
<testcaseroot>
  dimr_config.xml Configuration file, input for DIMR
  <fm>              Work directory for D-Flow FM
    foo.mdu          D-Flow FM input file
  <dflowfmoutput> D-Flow FM output directory
    foo_com.nc Communication file, written/read by both D-Flow FM and D-Waves
  <rtc>             Work directory for D-RTC
    settings.json D-RTC input file (must have exactly this name)
  <xml_dir>        D-RTC directory containing xml input/output files and csv output file
  <xsd_dir>        D-RTC directory containing xsd input files
  <wave>           Work directory for D-Waves
    foo.mdw          D-Waves input file
  TMP_ESMF*_source.nc Temporary input file for ESMF_Regridder, created by D-Waves
  TMP_ESMF*_destination.nc Temporary input file for ESMF_Regridder, created by D-Waves
  TMP_ESMF*_weights.nc Resulting weights file, created by ESMF_Regridder, read by D-Waves
  PET0.RegridWeightGen.Log ESMF_Regridder log file
  swn-diag.foo SWAN log file
```

### 18.6.7 SWAN output file as input to D-Flow FM

**Note:** This is of TRL level 1-3 (concept), with the definitions of the Technical Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) in Section 2.7.

![](_page_306_Picture_6.jpeg)

Instead of coupling D-Flow FM to D-Waves, a SWAN output file, in NetCDF format, can be used. Space and time varying data can be read and used as input. Currently this method can be used to add (wave related) bed shear stress to the D-Water Quality simulation inside D-Flow FM, and to add wave forcing and bed shear stress contributions to a 2DH D-Flow FM model (`wavemodelnr = 7`).

#### *Passing information to D-Water Quality*

Currently, the following input specification is accepted in the `ExtForceFile` and the `.mdu` file:

Example old style `ExtForceFile`:

```
  * comments
  * comments  QUANTITY                                                       = wavesignificantheight
  FILENAME                                                       = swanout.nc
  VARNAME                                                               = sea_surface_wave_significant_height
  FILETYPE                                                               = 11
  METHOD                                                                   = 3
  EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD                                                  = 1
  OPERAND                                                                  = 0  QUANTITY                                                                      = waveperiod
  FILENAME                                                                   = swanout.nc
  VARNAME                                                                        = tps
  FILETYPE                                                                   = 11
  METHOD                                                                         = 3
```

```
EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD = 1
OPERAND                = 0
```

Where the quantities (wavesignificant height and waveperiod) are dictated by D-Flow FM and the varnames (sea\_surface\_wave\_significant\_height and tps) are chosen by SWAN in its NetCDF output file.

Example lines in .mdu file:

```
[waves]
Wavemodelnr          = 7      # 0: none,
                          1: fetch/depth limited hurdlestive,
                          2: Young-Verhagen,
                          3: SWAN via D-Waves,
                          5: uniform,
                          7: SWAN-NetCDFRouwav                  = FR84
FlowWithoutWaves       = true # True: Do not use Wave data in the flow computations,
                                it will only be passed through to D-WAQWaveSwartDelwaq       = 1
```

Currently, only the combination of parameters in the example above is tested.

**Note:** An example model, with run scripts, is included in the (open source) code. After registering yourself at <https://oss.deltares.nl/>, you can have a look at: [https://svn.oss.deltares.nl/repos/delft3d/trunk/examples/12\\_dflowfm/test\\_data/FriesianInlet\\_schematic\\_SWAN\\_nc/FM](https://svn.oss.deltares.nl/repos/delft3d/trunk/examples/12_dflowfm/test_data/FriesianInlet_schematic_SWAN_nc/FM)

**Note:** The previous example used to require Wavemodelnr = 6. This mode has now been merged with Wavemodelnr = 7. If you specify Wavemodelnr = 6 in the mdu-file, this will be automatically adjusted for you.

#### Forcing flow in D-Flow FM

Depending on the [waves] waveforcing keyword, different wave quantities are required to be specified in the (old-style) external forcing file (Table 18.4) in case you want to use offline wave information to force the flow. For every Waveforcing value, *every* variable needs to be present in the ExtForceFile for the functionality to work. Note that you have to provide the variable name of the significant wave height together with the wave direction in order to interpolate the directions correctly. You can do this as follows:

Example lines in .mdu file:

```
[waves]
Wavemodelnr           = 7
Rouwav                 = FR84
Waveforcing           = 1
```

Example lines in (old-style) .ext file:

```
QUANTITY                                             = wavedirection
FILENAME                                            = output_swan2D_permuted.nc
VARNAME                                            = sea_surface_wave_from_direction sea_surface_wave_significant_height
FILETYPE                                            = 11
METHOD                                              = 3
EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD                              = 1
OPERAND                                            = 0QUANTITY                                             = waveperiod
FILENAME                                            = output_swan2D_permuted.nc
VARNAME                                            = tm01
FILETYPE                                            = 11
METHOD                                              = 3
EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD                              = 1
OPERAND                                            = 0QUANTITY                                             = wavesignificantheight
FILENAME                                            = output_swan2D_permuted.nc
VARNAME                                            = sea_surface_wave_significant_height
FILETYPE                                            = 11
METHOD                                              = 3
EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD                              = 1
OPERAND                                            = 0QUANTITY                                             = xwaveforce
FILENAME                                            = output_swan2D_permuted.nc
VARNAME                                            = eastward_wave_force
FILETYPE                                            = 11
METHOD                                             = 3
EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD                              = 1
OPERAND                                            = 0QUANTITY                                             = ywaveforce
FILENAME                                            = output_swan2D_permuted.nc
VARNAME                                            = northward_wave_force
FILETYPE                                            = 11
METHOD                                            = 3
EXTRAPOLATION_METHOD                             = 1
OPERAND                                            = 0
```

In this way, the change in momentum due to the presence of waves can be accounted for by using the spatial radiation stress gradients ( $waveforcing=1$ ), the total dissipation ( $waveforcing=2$ ), or by distributing the wave pressure forces over the water column ( $waveforcing=3$ ). This is explained in section 3.8.

### 18.6.8 Parallel computations

See section 8.4 for running D-Flow FM in parallel using MPI via DIMR. When running a coupled D-Flow FM and D-Waves computation, SWAN is doing the actual wave computation. D-Waves takes care of the communication, synchronization and interpolation between D-Flow FM and SWAN using files.

By default the OpenMP version of SWAN is used and SWAN will start as many threads as there are cores on the computational node being used. The user can change the number of threads by specifying environmental parameter OMP\_NUM\_THREADS\_SWAN in the command box executing the computation, e.g. on Windows:

```
set OMP_NUM_THREADS_SWAN=4
```

**Table 18.4:** Entries in ExtForceFile for use with wavemodel 7. The entries in the Varname column that should be present in the NetCDF file depend on the Waveforcing value in the .mdu file.

| Waveforcing | Quantity                        | Varname                                        |
|-------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| 1           | wavedirection                   | theta0                                         |
|             | waveperiod                      | sea_surface_wave_from_direction                |
|             | waveheight                      | any valid period field                         |
|             | waveforce                       | sea_surface_wave_significant_height            |
|             | waveforce                       | eastward_wave_force                            |
| 2           | wavedirection                   | theta0                                         |
|             | waveperiod                      | sea_surface_wave_from_direction                |
|             | waveheight                      | any valid period field                         |
|             | totalwavedissipation            | sea_surface_wave_significant_height            |
|             | total_energy_dissipation        | total_energy_dissipation                       |
| 3           | wavedirection                   | theta0                                         |
|             | waveperiod                      | sea_surface_wave_from_direction                |
|             | waveheight                      | any valid period field                         |
|             | waveforce                       | sea_surface_wave_significant_height            |
|             | waveforce                       | eastward_wave_force                            |
|             | wavebreakerdissipation          | northward_wave_force                           |
|             | whitecappingdissipation         | depth_induced_surf_breaking_energy_dissipation |
|             | whitecapping_energy_dissipation |                                                |

```
export OMP_NUM_THREADS_SWAN=4
```

When D-Flow FM runs in parallel using MPI, the wave configuration is not changed: there's still one instance of D-Waves taking care of the communication, synchronization and interpolation between multiple D-Flow FM instances and the OpenMP version of SWAN. The D-Flow FM instances might be spread over multiple computational nodes. Both D-Waves and SWAN will run on the main/first node. At some point, the single D-Waves instance will become the performance bottleneck in computations in which both D-Flow FM runs in parallel (using MPI, possibly on multiple nodes) and SWAN runs in parallel (using OpenMP on the main node only). There is no workaround yet.

Alternatively, it is possible to run SWAN as a library inside multiple D-Waves MPI instances, see section 18.6.10 for instructions. Then both D-Flow FM and SWAN will run in parallel using MPI, but all D-Waves tasks (communication, synchronization, interpolation) are still performed by the single master instance. Then, advantages are:

- ◇ On some clusters a performance issue might occur, see section 18.6.9. This issue can be circumvented with this approach.
- ◇ The performance might increase since all nodes reserved for the computation are used both the D-Flow FM computation and the SWAN computation.

**Table 18.5:** Example computation times of a testcase coupling D-Flow FM (parallel MPI) with SWAN (parallel OMP/MPI)

|                          | # cores | # FM partitions | # SWAN partitions | Wall clock time | Resource waste |
|--------------------------|---------|-----------------|-------------------|-----------------|----------------|
| Assumed optimal          | 4       | 4 MPI           | 4 OMP             | 5.5             | 323%           |
| Over allocated resources | 8       | 4 MPI           | 4 OMP             | 1.3             | 100%           |
| Workaround               | 4       | 4 MPI           | 4 MPI             | 2.1             | 62%            |
| Assumed ideal situation  | 4       | 4 MPI           | 4 OMP             | 1.3             | 0%             |

And a disadvantage and restriction is:

- ◇ The MPI parallelization of SWAN is performing not as well as the OpenMP implementation.

### 18.6.9 Check efficiency of parallel FLOW-WAVE computation

In parallel FLOW-WAVE computations, D-Flow FM is using MPI and SWAN is using OpenMP by default. When the D-Flow FM instances are carrying out computations, then the SWAN processes are idle and vice versa. It might occur that idle D-Flow FM instances occupy 100% of the cores, blocking them from being used by the SWAN threads. It can occur both on Windows and Linux, but this does not show up in the Delft3D 4 Suite. [section 18.6.10](#) contains a workaround based on running SWAN as a library in D-Waves, using MPI. This section describes how to check whether you are hitting this problem.

Carry out two test runs:

1. 1 Assumed optimal usage  
   Use for example a 4 core machine for a D-Flow FM simulation with 4 MPI partitions, running online with D-Waves, with `export OMP_NUM_THREADS_SWAN=4`, forcing `SWAN_OMP` to use 4 threads. When D-Flow FM is computing, SWAN is idle and D-Flow FM can use the 4 cores. When SWAN is computing, D-Flow FM is idle and should not use the 4 cores.
2. 2 Over allocated resources  
   Use for example a 8 core machine for the exact same computation (D-Flow FM with 4 MPI partitions, `export OMP_NUM_THREADS_SWAN=4`).

Expected results:

1. 1 If everything works as it should, the runtimes of both simulations should be similar (within a few percentages of difference).
2. 2 If you're hitting the above mentioned issue, the second computation is significantly faster than the first. The workaround in [section 18.6.10](#) might be useful.

Noted that Table 18.5 shows computation times on the Deltares cluster of an example testcase. Behaviour will vary depending on hardware, software and model specification.

**18.6.10 Run SWAN as a library inside D-Waves with MPI**This alternative might circumvent the performance problem described in section 18.6.8 and section 18.6.9. To run SWAN as a library inside multiple D-Waves MPI instances, apply the following two changes to your input files:

1. 1 In the DIMR configuration file, include in the fields for the wave component the following two tags:
   - ◇ `<process>`
     - listing all processes in which to run D-Waves/SWAN.
   - ◇ `<mpiCommunicator>`
     - specifying the name of the D-Waves mpi communicator variable that should always read `engine_comm_world`.

Example (with 5 MPI partitions):

```
component name="myNameWave">
<library>wave</library>
<workingDir>wave</workingDir>
<inputFile>f34.mdw</inputFile>
<process>0 1 2 3 4</process>
<mpiCommunicator>engine_comm_world</mpiCommunicator>
</component>
```

1. 2 In the mdw configuration file specify in the [General] block:

```
SwanMode = lib
```

Remarks:

- ◇ All data exchange, synchronization and interpolation between D-Flow FM and SWAN is (still) done by the master instance of D-Waves in a sequentially manner, being a potential scalability bottleneck.
- ◇ All (nested) SWAN domains will run on the same number of processes.
- ◇ This alternative also works when D-Waves runs standalone, without D-Flow FM. However, then it is necessary that DIMR is used to start the computation.
- ◇ In case you need to modify the SWAN input file after D-Waves has prepared it: this is still possible.

**18.7 Coupling with D-RTC (FBC-Tools)**This section is on the *coupling* of hydrodynamics and real-time control — more specific: feed-back control — of hydraulic structures.

**18.7.1 Introduction**A coupled flow-rtc model can be run either as an Integrated Model from within the D-Flow FM User Interface, or from the commandline using the DIMR program (Deltares Integrated Model Runner).

In case of a flow-rtc coupling

- ◇ the flow model will exchange for example *Water levels*
- ◇ subsequently, the rtc model will prescribe for example the *Crest level* of a controlled structure, based on the exchanged *water levels*
- ◇ in case of an *online* coupling this *Crest level* will influence the hydrodynamic simulation.

## 18.7.2 Getting started

### 18.7.2.1 User interface: the first steps

First, the user must add a *real-time control* model to the *flow-fm* model. The **Project** window will look like this.

![](_page_312_Picture_4.jpeg)

*Figure 18.1: An Integrated model in the Project window*

Secondly, the user will model the control flow for an hydraulic structure. This may look like this.

![](_page_312_Diagram_7.jpeg)

*Figure 18.2: Example of a Control flow in D-RTC*

Full documentation on D-RTC is available in its own User Manual. This section is limited to the details of running coupled flow-rtc models.

### 18.7.2.2 Input D-Flow FM

The hydraulic structures that are normally driven by scalar values or time series in `<*.bc>` files, will now be fed by D-RTC. Replace the timeseries file name by the `realtime` keyword in the `<structures.ini>` file (Appendix C.13):

```
[Structure]
type           = weir                                                            # Type of structure
id                 = weir01                                                          # Name of the structure
locationFile      = weir01.pli                                                    # *.pli; Polyline geometry definition for 2D structure
crestLevel         = realtime                                                          # Crest level in [m]
```

Also, the MDU file may optionally contain an observation file and/or a cross section file, such that D-RTC's triggers can be set to respond to the computed values at these locations.

```
[output]
ObsFile           = obs.xyn
CrsFile           = river_crs.pli
```

### 18.7.2.3 Input D-RTC

The input of D-RTC consists of several `<*.xml>` files and a toplevel `<settings.json>`. We refer to the D-RTC User Manual (Deltares, 2026d) for further details.

### 18.7.2.4 Input DIMR

In Section 18.6.4, details on a coupled flow-rtc-wave model are presented. This can serve as an example for a flow-rtc coupling, by leaving out all wave-related fragments.

### 18.7.2.5 Online process order

This is discussed in Section 18.6.5 for a coupled flow-rtc-wave model. This can serve as an example for a flow-rtc coupling, by leaving out all wave-related fragments.

## 18.8 Coupling with module for Sea Lock Exchange

### 18.8.1 Introduction

The Wanda-Locks software suite of Deltares is available for the simulation of salt intrusion in sea locks, and it can be coupled to Delft3D-FLOW via the COSUMO toolbox. However, this results into very computationally intensive simulations. Therefore, another approach has been developed that is much less computationally demanding, called D-SLE. D-Flow FM can be coupled to the "Sea Lock Exchange" software program of Deltares, which is called the "Zeesluisformulering" in Dutch. The D-SLE software is available in Python and as a C-library and has been applied to many sea locks. The technical documentation of D-SLE can be found at <https://libzsf.readthedocs.io/en/latest/theory/index.html>.

Based on the water level and the salinity concentration at lateral locations, discharges 'from sea to lake' and 'from lake to sea' are computed by the D-SLE. In D-Flow FM these discharges are modelled via laterals. The sea lock itself is represented in the D-Flow FM model area as a closed or dry area, as illustrated in Figure 18.3.

### 18.8.2 Coupling of D-Flow FM with D-SLE

A coupled D-Flow FM-D-SLE model can be run as an Integrated Model from within the D-Flow FM User Interface, or from a command prompt using the DIMR program (Deltares Integrated Model Runner).

In case of a coupled D-Flow FM-D-SLE model

- ◇ the D-Flow FM model and the D-SLE model exchange water discharge and salinity through *laterals*.
- ◇ the D-Flow FM model provides boundary conditions to the D-SLE model, i.e. water level and salinity at the lake and sea sides. The D-SLE model will in turn provide lateral input to the D-Flow FM model, i.e. the discharge extracted from and the discharge and salinity deposited to the lake and sea.
- ◇ laterals in D-Flow FM may consist of multiple grid cells. All exchanged data is aggregated into a single value per lateral before the exchange with D-SLE.
- ◇ in case of 3D models the exchange of water and salinity can be subdivided over multiple layers.
- ◇ it is advised to specify different lateral locations for inflow and outflow at both sides of the sea lock, to prevent unphysical mixing in the D-Flow FM model. This results into four laterals per sea lock.

### 18.8.3 Passive constituents and temperature

#### 18.8.3.1 Introduction

In addition to salinity, D-SLE supports the transport of *passive constituents* and temperature through the sea lock. Passive constituents (e.g. tracers, sediment concentrations) are transported by the same water volumes computed by the salt intrusion model but do not influence the density or flow field. Because of this, their transport behavior can be calculated using a simple volume mass balance approach, without the need to solve additional transport equations. While temperature is an input for the salt intrusion model and does influence density, it afterwards also behaves as a passive constituent.

The required DIMR keys for temperature and passive constituents are listed in Section 18.8.4, together with a full configuration example.

#### 18.8.3.2 Configuration in the D-SLE ini file

The initial concentrations of temperature and salinity inside the lock at the start of the simulation are specified in the D-SLE ini file using the following keyword:

```
[sealock]
id                                       = sealock_A
initial_salinity_lock                     = 10.0
initial_temperature_lock                  = 6.0
```

Currently, specifying initial constituent concentrations in the lock is only supported for temperature, but support for additional passive constituents can be added later if there is a user demand.

### 18.8.3.3 Transport calculation

The transport of passive constituents simply follows from a volume mass balance, using the water discharges computed by the salt intrusion model. However this is calculated differently in the two transport modes of D-SLE, and also differs from the salinity transport during a flush-with-doors-closed phase, as described below.

#### 18.8.3.3.1 Cycle-average mode

In cycle-average mode, D-SLE derives a salinity mixing fraction for each output side, representing the proportion of sea water in the outflow:

$$f = \frac{S_{\text{out}} - S_{\text{lake}}}{S_{\text{sea}} - S_{\text{lake}}}, \quad (18.1)$$

where  $S_{\text{out}}$  is the salinity computed by D-SLE for that output side. The same fraction is applied to every passive constituent:

$$c_{\text{out}} = c_{\text{lake}} + f(c_{\text{sea}} - c_{\text{lake}}). \quad (18.2)$$

This is analytically exact for passive tracers at hydrodynamic steady state: the sea-water fraction in the outflow is a purely hydraulic property, so any passive tracer follows it linearly. When  $S_{\text{sea}} = S_{\text{lake}}$ , the fraction defaults to zero and all constituents output the lake-side boundary value.

#### 18.8.3.3.2 Phase-wise mode

In phase-wise mode, constituent transport uses a volume mass balance on the lock chamber for each phase. For the levelling and gate-open phases (routines 1–4), the post-phase lock concentration is:

$$c_{\text{lock,new}} = \frac{c_{\text{lock}} V_{\text{before}} + c_{\text{lake}} V_{\text{from lake}} + c_{\text{sea}} V_{\text{from sea}} - c_{\text{lock}} V_{\text{to lake}} - c_{\text{lock}} (V_{\text{to sea}} - V_{\text{flush}}) - c_{\text{lake}} V_{\text{flush}}}{V_{\text{after}}}, \quad (18.3)$$

where  $V_{\text{flush}}$  is the flushing passthrough volume: water that traverses the lock from lake to sea without mixing, entering and exiting at the lake boundary concentration. The outflow concentration to the lake equals the pre-phase lock concentration; the outflow concentration to the sea is the volume-weighted average of the lock and passthrough contributions.

#### 18.8.3.3.3 Flush-with-doors-closed (routine $< 0$ )

During a flush-with-doors-closed phase, the lock volume is constant (doors remain closed) and a pump forces water from the lake through the lock to the sea. Passive constituents are modelled using an analytical continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR) model:

$$c_{\text{lock}}(t) = c_{\text{lake}} + (c_{\text{lock},0} - c_{\text{lake}}) e^{-\lambda t}, \quad \lambda = \frac{Q}{V_{\text{lock}}}, \quad (18.4)$$

where  $c_{\text{lake}}$  is the lake-side boundary concentration,  $c_{\text{lock},0}$  is the constituent concentration in the lock at the start of the phase,  $Q$  is the flushing discharge and  $V_{\text{lock}}$  is the lock volume. The decay rate  $\lambda = Q/V$  is always positive, ensuring the constituent always converges towards the lake boundary value regardless of whether  $c_{\text{lock},0}$  is above or below  $c_{\text{lake}}$ .

![](_page_316_Figure_1.jpeg)

**Figure 18.3:** An example of a simple D-Flow FM model in the Graphic User Interface (GUI). The sea lock is in the middle, the lake on the left side and the sea on the right side.

### 18.8.3.4 Difference from salinity during flush-with-doors-closed

The salinity model in D-SLE uses a different decay formulation during flush-with-doors-closed that accounts for density stratification effects:

$$\lambda_{\text{sal}} = \frac{Q(S_{\text{lock}} - S_{\text{lake}})}{M_{\text{salt,lock}}}, \quad (18.5)$$

where  $S_{\text{lock}}$  and  $S_{\text{lake}}$  are the salinity concentrations (in ppt) of the lock and the lake respectively, and  $M_{\text{salt,lock}}$  is the total salt mass in the lock. As a consequence, a passive constituent configured to mirror salinity will *not* produce results identical to salinity during a flush-with-doors-closed phase, unless  $S_{\text{lake}} = 0$ . In that special case,  $M_{\text{salt,lock}} = S_{\text{lock}} V_{\text{lock}}$ , so  $\lambda_{\text{sal}}$  reduces to  $Q/V_{\text{lock}}$ , identical to the volumetric  $\lambda$  used for passive constituents. For any non-zero lake salinity the two formulations diverge, because the salt-mass-dependent  $\lambda_{\text{sal}}$  differs from the volumetric  $\lambda = Q/V$ .

In practice this difference is small for typical flushing durations and discharge rates. It reflects the physical fact that salt transport during flushing is influenced by density stratification effects that do not apply to dissolved passive tracers.

### 18.8.4 Configuration of the model

#### 18.8.4.1 Input D-Flow FM

Figure 18.3 shows a simple D-Flow FM model in which a sea lock is located in the middle of a D-Flow FM model domain. The cells with red triangles represent the sea lock via dry points in D-Flow FM and are therefore non-computational cells; note that it is also possible to represent dry points by simply removing the grid cells. In this example the lake is on the left and the sea on the right side of the model. There are four lateral locations, denoted by four blue polygons. For both the lake side and the sea side the lateral locations for inflow and outflow are separated. In this example, all four laterals consists of two grid cells.

Remark: for administrative reasons it is necessary that the polygons for each lateral are in separate polygon-files. When using the GUI to create a model this is automatically correct, but the user should pay attention to this when creating or modifying a model by hand.

```
[lateral]
Id                                         = discharge_from_lake
locationFile                                = discharge_from_lake.pol
discharge                                  = realtime
applyTransport                            = 1
```

Note that here the parameter `discharge` and `applyTransport` should be set to `realtime` and 1, respectively. Keyword `realtime` indicates that the parameter receives its values from the coupled model (D-SLE in this example) and keyword `applyTransport=1` indicates that transport of salinity (or temperature or tracers) through the lateral is taken into account. The string of parameter `Id` will be used to identify the lateral in a DIMR configuration.

### 18.8.4.2 Input DIMR

A general description of DIMR configuration file structure can be found in 18.6.4. This section describes entries specific for coupling D-Flow FM and D-SLE.

Supported items for D-SLE as `<sourceName>` (D-SLE gives discharge and salinity as output, at the sea and lake sides, to deliver to D-Flow FM):

- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/discharge_from_sea`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/discharge_from_lake`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/discharge_to_sea`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/discharge_to_lake`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/salinity_to_sea`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/salinity_to_lake`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/temperature_to_sea`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/temperature_to_lake`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/constituent_to_sea_name (optional, for passive constituents)`
- ◇ `results/sealock_ID/constituent_to_lake_name (optional, for passive constituents)`

Supported items for D-SLE as `<targetName>` (D-SLE receives boundary conditions from D-Flow FM):

- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/head_lake`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/salinity_lake`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/temperature_lake`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/water_volume_from_lake` (only required for 3D model)
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/water_volume_to_lake` (only required for 3D model)
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/head_sea`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/salinity_sea`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/temperature_sea`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/water_volume_from_sea` (only required for 3D model)
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/water_volume_to_sea` (only required for 3D model)
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/constituent_lake_name (optional, for passive constituents)`
- ◇ `dsle_boundary_condition/sealock_ID/constituent_sea_name (optional, for passive constituents)`

Supported items for D-Flow FM as `<sourceName>` (D-Flow FM provides boundary conditions to D-SLE):

- ◇ `laterals/lateral_ID/outgoing/water_level`
- ◇ `laterals/lateral_ID/outgoing/water_salinity`

- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/outgoing/water\_temperature
- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/outgoing/water\_volume (only required for 3D model)
- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/constituents/name (*optional, for passive constituents*)

Supported items for D-Flow FM as <targetName> (D-Flow FM receives discharge and salinity from D-SLE):

- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/water\_discharge
- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/incoming/water\_salinity
- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/incoming/water\_temperature
- ◇ laterals/lateral\_ID/incoming/name (*optional, for passive constituents*)

The `sealock_ID` is the ID of the sea lock specified in the <.ini> file of D-SLE, `lateral_ID` is the ID of the lateral specified in the <.ext> file of D-Flow FM, and *name* refers to the constituent name as used in the D-Flow FM model. The other keywords are fixed. For depth-varying quantities in 3D models, the item `type` should be set to "`pointer`".

Note that the time interval in element <time> should be a multiple of `DtUser` specified in <.mdu>. An example of a DIMR config file for a 3D setup with one sea lock with ID `sealock_A`, including temperature and a passive constituent named `foo`, is given below.

The `sealock_ID` is ID of the sea-lock specified in the <.ini> file of D-SLE and `lateral_ID` ID of the lateral specified in the <.ext> of D-Flow FM. The other keywords are fixed.

Note that the time interval in element <time> should be a multiple of `DtUser` specified in <.mdu>. Note also that for depth-varying quantities in 3D models, the item `type` should be set to "`pointer`". An example of a DIMR config file can be found below for a 3D setup with one sea lock with ID `sealock_A`, including temperature and a passive constituent named `foo`.

### 18.8.4.3 Input D-SLE

At least two input files are required to configure a D-SLE model: an `<.ini>` file containing various information about the sea locks and a `<.csv>` file containing operational parameters of the sea lock. For a setting with more than one sea lock, for each sea lock a separated operational parameters `<.csv>` file should be provided.

**Table 18.6:** Input parameters in `<.ini>` file.

| Parameter name                     | Description                                                                                                                                    |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| <code>start_time</code>            | Mandatory. This should be equal or later than the first time level specified in the operational parameters <code>&lt;.csv&gt;</code> file      |
| <code>kmx</code>                   | Only for 3D model. This specifies the maximum number of layers of the D-Flow FM model, as also specified in the <code>&lt;.mdu&gt;</code> file |
| <code>log_level</code>             | Optional. To specify level of logging.                                                                                                         |
| <code>id</code>                    | Mandatory. To specify the identity of a sea lock, to be used in DIMR configuration.                                                            |
| <code>computation_mode</code>      | Mandatory. Either <code>phase_wise</code> or <code>cycle_average</code> .                                                                      |
| <code>initial_head_lock</code>     | Initial water level in the sea lock.                                                                                                           |
| <code>initial_salinity_lock</code> | Initial salinity in the sea lock.                                                                                                              |

| Parameter name                           | Description                                                                                                                                                                              |
|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| <i>(continued from previous page)</i>    |                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| <code>initial_temperature_lock</code>    | Initial water temperature in the sea lock.                                                                                                                                               |
| <code>initial_volume_ship_in_lock</code> | ship volume in the sea lock.                                                                                                                                                             |
| <code>lock_length</code>                 | Length of the sea lock.                                                                                                                                                                  |
| <code>lock_width</code>                  | Width of the sea lock.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| <code>lock_bottom</code>                 | Depth of the sea lock.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| <code>flow_profile</code>                | Only for 3D model. It specifies flow profile over depth used to determine to which layers water should be pumped in and from which layers water should be extracted. See 18.8.5.         |
| <code>allowed_head_difference</code>     | Optional. Default = 10 cm. Allowed remaining water level difference when opening doors between lock and lake/sea. If the difference is larger than this value, the simulation will stop. |

Example of an `<.ini>` file containing two sea locks:

```
[general]
start_time                                        = 200101010000
kmx                                             = 5
log_level                                          = debug[sealock]
id                                                     = sealock_A
computation_mode                                    = phase_wise
sealock_operational_parameters                   = sealock_A.csv

initial_salinity_lock                               = 10.0
initial_temperature_lock                          = 6.0
initial_volume_ship_in_lock                     = 0.0
lock_length                                        = 300.0
lock_width                                        = 25.0
lock_bottom                                      = -7.0

id                                                     = sealock_B
computation_mode                                  = phase_wise
sealock_operational_parameters               = sealock_B.csv
initial_head_lock                               = 1.0
initial_salinity_lock                             = 15.0
initial_temperature_lock                        = 6.0
initial_volume_ship_in_lock                    = 0.0
lock_length                                      = 500.0
lock_width                                      = 70.0
lock_bottom                                     = -18.0
```

### 18.8.5 Processing of the received lateral data items in D-Flow FM

In this section, we describe the processing of the lateral data items in D-Flow FM. D-SLE expects and returns a single value per lateral and per layer. In D-Flow FM, in the horizontal direction, the single value from D-SLE will be distributed over all cells in the lateral after exchange with D-SLE. In turn, the values of all the cells will be aggregated before exchanging them to D-SLE.
